Jordan’s Economy Feels Strain as Respiratory Virus Epidemic Prompts Nationwide Closures

Amman — The Jordanian government has implemented sweeping closures and movement restrictions across the country as part of efforts to contain the spread of a fast-moving respiratory virus, a move that has brought significant disruptions to the national economy and daily life. The epidemic, first identified in the capital city last month, has now led to the closure of schools, retail outlets, and most non-essential businesses, in addition to a nighttime curfew in all governorates.

Major industrial and service sectors have been affected, with energy firms among those reporting operational challenges. Jordan Petroleum Refinery Co, one of the country’s largest energy producers, announced on Sunday that it has reduced its output by nearly 40 percent due to falling demand and logistical difficulties resulting from the restrictions. “Our priority remains the health and safety of our employees and the wider community,” said company spokesperson Hanan Qawasmi. “We are coordinating closely with authorities to maintain essential fuel supplies, but the situation remains fluid.”

The Jordan Chambers of Industry has estimated that the economic slowdown could result in a 2.5 percent contraction in GDP this quarter if the restrictions continue. “Jordan is facing its most serious public health emergency in decades, and the impact on our manufacturers is already being felt,” said Adel Abu Hamdan, a board member of the Chambers. “We urge the government to consider targeted support for affected sectors, especially those that are critical to national infrastructure.”

Transport and logistics companies are also facing mounting challenges. An executive at East Gate Logistics, a major freight provider, reported a 60 percent drop in cargo movement through the country’s main highways and border crossings. “With curfews and partial closures, our delivery times have doubled, and some routes are completely suspended,” he said.

The Ministry of Health has defended the sweeping measures, citing a rise in confirmed cases and warnings from epidemiologists about potential hospital overcrowding. “We understand the hardship these steps cause, but protecting public health must come first,” said Dr. Rami Azzam, a senior official in the ministry. The government has pledged to review the restrictions weekly, depending on the epidemic’s trajectory.

Meanwhile, residents across Amman and other cities queued outside supermarkets and pharmacies before closures went into effect, as uncertainty over the duration of the lockdown persists. The Prime Minister has appealed for calm, assuring the public that essential supplies will be maintained throughout the crisis.
